Chapter one.

The rain had been falling since before dawn, and by the time the coach reached the bottom of the hill the road had turned into a river of brown mud. Nobody inside said a word.

12

She counted the boxes twice before she wrote the number down, because the last shipment had been short and nobody had noticed for a week.

He asked whether the bridge would hold another winter, and the engineer looked at the cracked stone for a long time. No. That was all he said before he walked back to the truck. She asked him again on the way home, and he only nodded. Yes. She had known it would come to that.
Hi. Hi. Blah blah. The two of them stood in the doorway grinning like children who had just broken a window and gotten away with it.
"Wait," he said. "No." She turned around anyway and kept walking toward the station, her bag swinging against her hip. "Fine," he called after her. "Go."
Stop. Look. Listen. The old railway crossing had no gates, only a faded sign, and every child in the village learned those three words before they learned to read.
The meeting ran long. Too long. Everyone agreed on that much, even the chairman, who had spent forty minutes describing a budget nobody had read. Then it was over. Finally.

Part two.

III.

The winter that followed was the coldest anyone could remember. Wells froze. Sheep died in the fields, and the river stopped moving for the first time in forty years.
